title: Congee
subtitle: Chinese rice porridge
excerpt: Congee is a deeply soothing rice porridge simmered low and slow until the grains dissolve into a silky, spoonable broth. It works as a restorative breakfast, a light supper, or a base for almost any topping you have to hand.
sourceNotes: Congee is eaten across East and Southeast Asia as a comforting breakfast or restorative meal. The long, slow simmer breaks down the rice into a silky porridge that absorbs the flavour of the stock.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Congee thickens as it sits. Make it ahead and loosen with a little stock or water when reheating.

content.text: The ratio of rice to liquid is what defines congee. Where plain boiled rice uses roughly a 1:2 ratio, congee uses 1:8 or even 1:10, and the long simmer does the rest. The grains swell, burst, and thicken the liquid into a texture that is somewhere between a very loose porridge and a light cream soup. Good stock makes a big difference here: the rice absorbs its flavour throughout the whole cook.

Top the congee with a soft-poached or soft-boiled egg for extra richness. Other classic toppings include sliced ginger, crispy fried shallots, and a drizzle of chilli oil. The spring onions and sesame oil added at the end are not optional: they lift what would otherwise be a flat, starchy finish.
Rinse the rice in cold water until the water runs fairly clear. This removes excess starch and prevents the congee from becoming gluey rather than silky.
Put the rice, chicken stock, and sliced ginger into a large saucepan. Bring to a boil over a medium-high hob, stirring occasionally to prevent the rice from catching on the base.

Once boiling, reduce the heat to the lowest setting. Place a lid on the pan, leaving it slightly ajar to let steam escape. Simmer for 45 to 55 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes or so. The congee is ready when the rice has completely broken down and the mixture is thick, creamy, and pourable.
If serving with eggs, bring a small pan of water to a gentle simmer. Lower in the eggs and cook for 6 minutes for a soft-set yolk, then transfer to cold water and peel.
Season the congee with the soy sauce. Ladle into deep bowls and finish each portion with a drizzle of sesame oil and the sliced spring onions. Add a halved egg to each bowl if using.

items.symptom: The congee is gluey and stodgy rather than silky
items.cause: The rice was not rinsed, or the heat was too high and the starch set before the grains could break down gradually.
items.fix: Always rinse the rice first. Keep the heat at the lowest possible setting and stir regularly. A little extra stock stirred in during cooking will loosen the texture.

items.symptom: The congee is still watery after an hour
items.cause: The heat was too low or the lid was fully on, slowing evaporation.
items.fix: Remove the lid entirely and increase the heat to a low simmer. Cook uncovered for a further 10 to 15 minutes, stirring frequently, until it thickens to your liking.

items.symptom: The rice has caught and scorched on the base
items.cause: The heat was too high or the pan was left without stirring for too long.
items.fix: Use a heavy-based pan to distribute heat more evenly, and stir every 10 minutes throughout the cook. Do not scrape up any scorched bits from the base.
